summary: This note surveys European Union law, covering the European Commission's role as the main executive body and its legislative monopoly, the division between constitutional and administrative law, and the rules on standing and direct effect. It also describes how fundamental rights entered EU law through the Court of Justice and the Charter of Fundamental Rights, the general principles developed by the Court, and the scope and nature of the EU's primary law treaties.
one_line: An overview of European Union law covering the Commission's powers, legal standing and direct effect, fundamental rights, general principles, and primary treaty law.
key_facts: Article 17(1) of the Treaty on European Union states the Commission should "promote the general interest of the Union".
Article 17(3) says Commissioners should be "completely independent" and not "take instructions from any Government".
Under Article 17(2), Union legislative acts may only be adopted on the basis of a Commission proposal, except where the Treaties provide otherwise.
Jean-Claude Juncker, an ex-Luxembourg Prime Minister, is described as the Commission's President and sets the agenda for the EU's work.
Since Ireland refused to consent to changes in the Treaty of Lisbon 2007, there remains one Commissioner for each of the 28 member states.
The proposal to make Commissioners be drawn from the elected Parliament was not adopted in the Treaty of Lisbon.
Under Directives, citizens or corporations were said in 1986 not to be allowed to bring claims against other non-state parties.
None of the original treaties establishing the European Union mention protection for fundamental rights.
In 1999 the European Council set up a body tasked with drafting a European Charter of Human Rights.

The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union draws on the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, the 1989 Declaration on Fundamental Rights produced by the European Parliament, and EU Treaties.
Accepted general principles of European Union Law include fundamental rights, proportionality, legal certainty, equality before the law and subsidiarity.
The primary law of the EU consists mainly of the founding treaties: the Treaty on European Union (TEU) and the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU).
The TEU specifically excludes certain regions, for example the Faroe Islands, from the jurisdiction of European Union law.
The Court of Justice of the European Union can interpret the Treaties, but it cannot rule on their validity, which is subject to international law.

entities.name: European Commission
entities.role: main executive body of the European Union with a monopoly on initiating the legislative procedure

entities.name: Treaty on European Union
entities.role: core EU treaty (TEU) whose Article 17 sets out the Commission's role and independence

entities.name: Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
entities.role: core EU treaty (TFEU) forming part of the primary law

entities.name: Jean-Claude Juncker
entities.role: Commission's President, described as an ex-Luxembourg Prime Minister, who sets the EU's agenda

entities.name: Federica Mogherini
entities.role: High Representative for Foreign and Security Policy, serving as a Commissioner

entities.name: Treaty of Lisbon
entities.role: treaty in which Ireland refused to consent to changes in 2007 and which did not adopt the proposal to draw Commissioners from Parliament

entities.name: Council
entities.role: described as the de facto catalyst of many legislative initiatives and approves Commissioners by qualified majority vote

entities.name: Parliament
entities.role: can formally request the Commission to submit a legislative proposal and gives majority approval to Commissioners

entities.name: Court of Justice
entities.role: European court that recognised fundamental rights as general principles of EU law and developed unwritten principles of EU law

entities.name: European Convention on Human Rights
entities.role: source for the Charter's list of fundamental rights, established in 1950 to prevent member states violating human rights

entities.name: European Court of Human Rights
entities.role: court whose jurisprudence informs the principles of EU law

entities.name: European Council
entities.role: set up a body in 1999 to draft a European Charter of Human Rights and may make specific provisions for regions under the TEU

entities.name: Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union
entities.role: list of fundamental rights drawn from several sources, intended to form a constitutional basis for the EU

entities.name: Declaration on Fundamental Rights
entities.role: declaration produced by the European Parliament in 1989, one source for the Charter

entities.name: Gibraltar
entities.role: territory where EU law applies because a member state is responsible for external relations; customs provisions made by the European Council

entities.name: Åland islands
entities.role: territory where EU law applies because a member state is responsible for external relations

entities.name: Faroe Islands
entities.role: region specifically excluded from the jurisdiction of EU law by the TEU

entities.name: Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon
entities.role: region for which the European Council made specific customs provisions

entities.name: Madeira
entities.role: island territory to which EU law applies

entities.name: Canary Islands
entities.role: island territory to which EU law applies
